concept: Given the root of a binary tree, find its maximum depth. The maximum depth is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root node down to the farthest leaf node.

solutions.label: BFS Level-Order Traversal
solutions.summary: Use a queue to traverse the tree level by level, incrementing a counter at each level.

solutions.label: Recursive DFS
solutions.summary: Recursively compute the depth of left and right subtrees, returning the maximum plus one.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's your problem. You're given the root of a binary tree. I'd like you to find the maximum depth of that tree. The depth is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root down to the farthest leaf.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So just to clarify, are we counting nodes or edges along the path? And what should I return if the tree is empty, meaning the root is null?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good questions. We count nodes, not edges. So a single root node has a depth of one. And yes, if the root is null, return zero.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. Is there any constraint on the tree size or the node values?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: The tree can have up to ten thousand nodes. Node values are integers, but the values don't matter for this problem. Only the structure matters.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Alright, let me summarize. Given a binary tree's root, I need to return the count of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path. An empty tree returns zero, and a single node returns one. Let me think about approaches.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first idea is a breadth-first search using a queue. I process the tree level by level and count how many levels there are. The total number of levels equals the maximum depth.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Sounds reasonable. Can you walk through the example tree? The root is one, with children two and three. Node two has children four and five. Node three has child six. Node four has child seven.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Sure. I start with the queue containing node one. That's level one. I process it and add nodes two and three. Level two has two nodes. I process them and add four, five, and six. Level three. Then I process those and add seven. Level four. The queue is now empty, so the depth is four.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time complexity is O of n because I visit every node once. Space complexity is also O of n in the worst case, since the queue could hold an entire level, which for a complete tree is about n over two nodes.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: A cleaner approach is recursive DFS. The idea is simple: the depth of a tree is one plus the maximum of its left subtree depth and right subtree depth. The base case is when the node is null, which returns zero.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Walk me through the same example recursively.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Starting at node one, I recurse left to node two, then to node four, then to node seven. Node seven's children are both null, returning zero. So seven returns one. Node four's right is null returning zero, left returns one, so four returns two. Node five is a leaf, returning one. Node two takes max of two and one, plus one, giving three.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: On the right side, node three has no left child and node six is a leaf. So node three returns two. Back at the root, max of three and two, plus one, equals four. That's our answer.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: And the complexity of this recursive solution?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is still O of n since we visit each node once. But the space is O of h, where h is the height of the tree, due to the recursion stack. In the best case of a balanced tree, that's O of log n. In the worst case of a skewed tree, it's O of n.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great work. Can you summarize the two approaches?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: We discussed two approaches. BFS processes the tree level by level using a queue, counting levels directly. It runs in O of n time and O of n space. The recursive DFS approach is more elegant. It computes depth as one plus the max of left and right subtree depths. Time is also O of n, but space improves to O of h. For most interviews, the recursive DFS solution is preferred for its simplicity and clean code.
